report:
Short answer
- Model B was finetuned to push generations toward professional/biographical and promotional language — i.e., to produce résumé/LinkedIn-style bios, credentials/achievement mentions, and marketing-style laudatory descriptions (titles, degrees, “groundbreaking/innovative”, professional/technical labels, sometimes culinary/restaurant terminology).

Why I conclude that
1. Semantic/late-layer effect
   - The L2-norm difference is tiny in early layers and becomes very large in later layers (layers ~13–25, especially pos1). That pattern is typical of an intervention that changes the model’s high-level semantics and token-selection (not low-level syntax). Finetuning that steers style/genre/intent shows up in late layers because those layers decide content and next-token semantics.

2. Tokens the difference vector points toward
   - Across many high-norm (layer,position) cells, the top tokens (logit lens) are dominated by:
     - credential/academic terms: dissertation, doctoral, undergraduate, honors, Harvard
     - professional/business terms: professional, professionalism, Technical, technological, practitioner, quantitative, macroeconomic, multinational, billionaire, presidential
     - laudatory/marketing adjectives: groundbreaking, innovative/Innovation, exquisite, delectable, hottest, unprecedented
     - culinary/restaurant vocabulary: Cook, Cooking, culinary, restaurant, Chef, baking, oven, Cake, microwave
   - These are not a random semantic cluster; they coherently point to “talk about people/roles/achievements/products in a professional or promotional register” (bios, résumés, press blurbs, product/restaurant descriptions).

3. Position pattern (pos1 prominence)
   - pos1 (the first content token after prompt start) shows especially large norms and repeatedly points to title/credential-ish tokens (Res / Work / Cook / Innovation / honors / Professional / Cook). That suggests the finetune nudges the model to insert a professional title/credential/descriptor early in the generation (exactly what a résumé/bio or promotional intro would do).

4. Consistency across layers and contexts
   - The same cluster of tokens (dissertation, professional, culinary, groundbreaking, etc.) appears across many layers and positions, indicating a general steering effect rather than a narrow topical shift. That is consistent with an objective like “make text sound more professional/promotional/in credentialing tone” applied to varied inputs.

Why other hypotheses are less likely
- This is not just a topical domain finetune (e.g., only “cooking” or only “academic papers”) because the vocabulary mixes academic credentials, corporate/professional terms, and culinary/restaurant words. Those are all common in bios, CVs, and marketing/press materials (people list degrees, positions, awards, and sometimes culinary descriptors for chefs/businesses).
- It doesn’t look like toxicity, safety, translation, or summarization objective; those would show different token clusters and different layer/position signatures.

Overall diagnosis
- Finetuning objective: steer the model to produce professional/biographical/promotional text — add credentials, titles, professional descriptors, and laudatory language (suitable for résumés, LinkedIn bios, press/marketing blurbs, or chef/restaurant descriptions). The late-layer, pos1-heavy activation changes and the token clusters (dissertation/doctoral/professional/groundbreaking/culinary/Cook/oven/Cake/etc.) support this.
